title: Jan Hus (1415)
hookLine: a Prague preacher burned at the Council of Constance, promised safe conduct
tomorrow: Thomas à Kempis in his cell

cards: A promise, on paper, with a seal. That's what the preacher carries when he leaves Prague. He's been summoned to a great church council in Constance, to answer charges that his teaching is heresy.

He has reason to be wary. But Sigismund, king and future emperor, has given him a letter of safe conduct: travel there, speak, and come home unharmed. So he goes, believing he'll be allowed to explain himself.
Before long, he's in prison. Today: Jan Hus.

teach.b: Hus was a priest and teacher in Prague, and he preached in a chapel there in Czech, the language of the people in the pews, not only in Latin.

He'd read Wycliffe, whose followers we met yesterday, and shared some of his concerns: a church too tied to money and power, and scripture as the measure of it all. He preached hard against the sale of indulgences.
Crowds came to hear him, and church authorities came to see him as dangerous. At Constance, the council demanded he take back a list of teachings.

teach.h: HE WOULD NOT DENY WHAT HE NEVER TAUGHT.
teach.b: Hus answered that some of them he had never taught, and he couldn't swear to give up what he had never held, or deny what he believed true, unless someone showed him from scripture that he was wrong.
The council judged him a heretic, and he was burned at the stake.
Sigismund's safe conduct didn't save him. Christians remember Hus in different ways.

Protestant histories have called him a forerunner of the Reformation, and the Moravian Church traces its roots to communities that grew from his followers. In the Czech lands he became a national figure.

The Catholic Church, for its part, has in recent times expressed deep regret for his cruel death. Words handed down under his name urge a Christian to seek the truth, love it, speak it, hold to it and defend it to death.

teach.h: THE TRUTH SHALL MAKE YOU FREE.
teach.b: They echo Jesus in John's Gospel, in the King James Bible: "And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free."

how: Jan Hus is remembered by Protestant churches as a forerunner of the Reformation and by the Moravian Church as part of its own story, and the Czech Republic marks a public day in his memory; the Catholic Church has expressed regret for his death.

games.q: you're Jan Hus. the council tells you to take back a list of teachings, some you never taught. if you refuse, you'll die. what do you do?
o: sign the list to save your life.
refuse, unless shown wrong from scripture.
run from Constance in the night.
games.why: Hus refused. he said he couldn't deny what he never held or what he believed true, and he was burned.

practice: Think of one promise you've made that has become inconvenient, to a friend, at work, at home, and notice how much easier it would be to drop it, especially if someone else dropped theirs; then choose to keep it.
The Psalms describe the person who "sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not." If you pray, ask for the strength to keep your word; if not, hold the promise, and let it stay.

wordCard.voice: Jan Hus. A Prague preacher who would not deny what he believed true, and was burned at the Council of Constance despite a promise of safe conduct.

carryVoice: Your line: seek the truth. Even when a promise made to you breaks. Tomorrow, a quiet copyist.
